intro.context: A sphere cannot be flattened without distortion. Projections make different choices about area, angles and shape, giving world maps different outlines.
intro.robinson.lead: A balanced view of the whole world.
intro.robinson.geometry: Parallels are horizontal and shorten toward the poles. Meridians curve except at the center, producing curved sides; each pole is a short line. Robinson used visual trials to set a table of widths and spacing at different latitudes, with interpolation between them.
intro.robinson.tradeoff: This compromise preserves neither area nor local angles. It distributes distortion rather than removing it, and high latitudes are still enlarged. Moving a region to the center changes its shape, but does not remove its area error.
intro.robinson.use: Browse global patterns and relative locations. For comparing region areas, switch to Equal Earth.
intro.robinson.observe: Follow the parallels toward the poles: how do they shorten, and how do the meridians bend?
intro.equalEarth.lead: Area proportions match the real world.
intro.equalEarth.geometry: Parallels are horizontal, poles are short lines, and most meridians curve, much like Robinson. Mathematical formulas coordinate horizontal width and vertical spacing so every small patch of the sphere is mapped at the same area ratio.
intro.equalEarth.tradeoff: Equal area preserves size ratios, not unchanged shapes. Regions can stretch or flatten; angles and distances change too. Similar outlines do not imply the same area properties.
intro.equalEarth.use: Compare region sizes or show global distributions that need accurate area proportions.
intro.equalEarth.observe: Switch to Mercator and back, comparing the apparent sizes of Greenland and Africa.
intro.mercator.lead: Local angles are preserved; high-latitude areas grow.
intro.mercator.geometry: Meridians are equally spaced vertical lines; every parallel is as wide as the equator. To preserve local angles, vertical scale increases by the same factor, spreading parallels farther apart toward the poles and producing a rectangular outline.
intro.mercator.tradeoff: Local angles are preserved, but large shapes and areas are distorted. On spherical Mercator, the length scale at 60° is twice that at the equator, making area four times as large. The poles lie at infinity; this map stops at about 85.05° north and south.
intro.mercator.use: Lines of constant compass bearing are straight. This is useful for expressing a constant heading, usually not the shortest route. Use an equal-area projection to compare world regions by area.
intro.mercator.observe: Compare parallel spacing: are 0°–30° and 30°–60° equally far apart on the map?
